messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Fwd: [stan-users] schools ranking problem using Stan and JAGS
parts:
Brilliant! Works like a charm. This is much better
converging and much better mixing once converged. Roughly
1 effective sample every 1--3 draws across all parameters.

I'll try to make this standard operating procedure.

It's a little less intensive on the multiplies with

diag_pre_multiply(sigma_Sigma, L_Sigma) * z

instead of

diag_pre_multiply(sigma_Sigma, L_Sigma * z)

because they are (3 x 1), (3 x 3) and (3 x M) respectively.
Eigen's clever enough to figure this all out on its own
using expression templates, but Stan's not that clever.

It would be more efficient with a diag_pre_multiply_lower_tri()
function. In fact, we pretty much need a whole bunch of
specializations of matrix ops for:

diagonal matrices (as vectors)
symmetric matrices
lower-triangular (upper-triangular) matrices
symmetric, positive definite matrices
correlation matrices ?

This is a nice modular project someone could take on a little
bit at a time that'd make a big difference in multivariate modeling
speed.

Here's the full Ben trick, isolated for inspection:

parameters {
matrix[3,M] z;
vector[3] gamma;
cholesky_factor_corr[3] L_Sigma;
vector<lower=0>[3] sigma_Sigma;
...
transformed parameters {
matrix[M,3] alpha;
alpha <- transpose(rep_matrix(gamma,M)
+ diag_pre_multiply(sigma_Sigma, L_Sigma) * z);
}
model {
to_vector(z) ~ normal(0,1);


which produces the equivalent of


parameters {
vector[3] gamma;
cholesky_factor_corr[3] L_Sigma;
vector<lower=0>[3] sigma_Sigma;
matrix[M,3] alpha;
...
model {
alpha ~ multi_normal(gamma,
diag_matrix(sigma_Sigma)
* L_sigma
* L_sigma'
* diag_matrix(sigma_Sigma));


(I just wrote the latter version this way for clarity --- quad_form_diag
and multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose would be more efficient.)

Ideally, to make this standard practice, we'd want a function
with behavior defined by

vector ben_transform(vector mu,
vector sigma,
matrix L,
matrix z) {
// validate sizes
return transpose(rep_matrix(mu,cols(z))
+ diag_pre_multiply(sigma, L) * z);

}

But we could write it in C++ with the derivatives all done
analytically.

It's tempting, but I think not worthwhile to wrap the whole
thing up with the priors on L and sigma. For example, we've been
working with models that place distinct informative priors on elements
of sigma.

- Bob
